findings.title: projen majorVersion is 1 but the package has only ever published 0.x (latest 0.3.8)
findings.detail: RootConfig.ts sets majorVersion: 1 and prerelease: 'alpha', yet npm shows 50 published versions all in 0.x with no 1.x, no alpha, and only a 'latest' dist-tag. The config has never produced a shipped release. To make the v3 redesign version 1.0.0-alpha (decision D6), main's majorVersion must move to 0 to avoid a release-branch major collision — which also aligns the config with the actually-published 0.x line. Confirm the maintainer's intent for the current line before changing main's release config or enabling the v3 release branch.

findings.title: The asciinema-recorder skill only documents interactive shell-wrapping, not the scripted recording + mp4 export this repo's milestone proofs need
findings.detail: Decision D3 says to build the milestone recorder on the user's asciinema-recorder skill. The skill's actual workflow is 'exit your agent, wrap your shell in asciinema rec, work normally' and it assumes brew/apt for installation. A milestone gate has to produce its proof unattended, so test/proof/record-demo.sh uses 'asciinema rec --command <script>' instead, and the skill documents no cast->mp4 export path at all (no agg/ffmpeg). The recorder built here works and is self-contained, so nothing is blocked. Out of scope to fix because the skill lives outside this repo in a shared global skills directory and editing it would change behaviour for the user's other projects; the skill's own self-evolution policy would have it patched, so raise it with the maintainer rather than silently amending a shared file.

findings.title: npx projen compat is already failing with 64 pre-existing API-removal errors, so it cannot serve as the API-break tripwire
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md names 'npx projen compat' as the tripwire that guards the published multi-language API, and ground rule 1 relies on it. It currently exits 1 with 64 'has been removed' errors before any v3 work is added, so it reports nothing useful. Root cause looks like aws-cdk-lib version skew rather than a deliberate API change: the removals are overwhelmingly members this repo inherits from aws-cdk-lib rather than declares (propertyInjectors on many *Props structs, Stack.removeStackTag, Stack.env, and the .with() methods on IEncryptionKey/IParameterConstruct/IRepositoryStack). The dependency is declared as a caret range (aws-cdk-lib@^<cdkVersion>) while the lockfile resolves locally to exactly the range floor, so the published release was compiled against a newer minor that has those members and the local build is compared against an older one that does not. Confirmed unrelated to the v3 work: 0 of the 122 types in the generated .jsii assembly are sourced from src/v3, so the new module contributes nothing to the diff. Left unfixed because resolving it means moving a dependency version or curating a .compatignore (which does not exist yet) for the published 0.x line, both outside an additive v3 task. Consequence while it stays red: a genuine break in the v3 public surface introduced by m1-accessor or a later milestone would be indistinguishable from this noise, so treat compat as uninformative until it is fixed. Fix direction: align the resolved aws-cdk-lib with the version the last release was built against, re-diff, and only then add genuinely-accepted keys to a .compatignore.

findings.title: Exported bare functions compile fine but are silently dropped from the jsii assembly, so they do not exist for Python/Java/.NET consumers
findings.detail: jsii only models types, so a bare exported function is compiled by tsc and then omitted from the generated assembly with no error and no warning. Verified against the existing published surface: mergeCodeBuildOptions is exported from the package entry point via src/resource-providers, yet the generated .jsii contains zero entries for it. TypeScript consumers can call it; Python, Java and .NET consumers cannot see it at all. This is pre-existing on the current 0.x line, not introduced by v3, and it is a silent failure mode rather than a build break, which is why it has gone unnoticed. Recorded here because it is a trap for every future milestone: the v3 public barrel deliberately exports only classes, interfaces and enums for this reason, and anything that needs to be callable from a non-TS language has to be a static method on a class rather than a function. Fix direction for the existing case: decide whether mergeCodeBuildOptions is meant to be public, and if so move it onto a class; if not, stop exporting it from the entry point.

findings.title: applyDerivedDefaults silently discards an aws value that is present but not an object, repairing a typo from ambient env instead of reporting it
findings.detail: applyDerivedDefaults replaces a non-plain-object aws value with a fresh object and then fills it from the environment, so a config file that says aws as a bare string or a list has that value thrown away with no signal. If the caller's schema lists aws.accountId as a required key the mistake still fails closed with MISSING_KEY, but if it does not, the typo is silently repaired from CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/CDK_DEFAULT_REGION and the user never learns their config was ignored. Consistent with the deliberate, tested behaviour that a whole config document which is not an object falls back to base defaults, so it is not an inconsistency so much as an open design question. Left unfixed because reporting it honestly needs a fifth ConfigError kind for a type mismatch, and the m1-validation task scope is explicitly ConfigError with four kinds. Revisit when M3 resolves config for real stages, where a silently ignored aws block would be much more costly.

findings.title: The level0-app fixture omits the cdk.json context feature-flag block that real cdk init emits, so it synthesizes under legacy defaults
findings.detail: level0-app exists to prove Level-0 inertness against an untouched cdk init app, and its TypeScript is faithful: it imports only aws-cdk-lib and constructs, with no wrapper symbol anywhere. Its cdk.json, however, is three lines, whereas cdk init app --language typescript emits a large context block of feature flags (and also package.json, jest.config.js, test/ and a watch key). The fixture therefore synthesizes under default/legacy feature-flag behaviour rather than the behaviour a newly initialised user app actually gets. Harmless for the current deploy/assert/destroy lifecycle test, which only checks a stack and an SSM parameter. It becomes a silent divergence for any later milestone that compares a synthesized template against what a real user app would produce, which is exactly what the M2 injection and M3 deploy-time-synth gates do. Fix direction: paste the feature-flag context from a real cdk init of the pinned aws-cdk version, and note the version it came from so it can be refreshed deliberately. The absent package.json is a separate, deliberate choice (root node_modules resolution) and is not part of this finding.

findings.title: The orphan sweep's stack-age arithmetic depends on GNU date and aborts the whole sweep if a timestamp fails to parse
findings.detail: cmd_sweep computes each stack's age with an arithmetic expression that embeds a date -u -d command substitution. The -d flag is GNU-specific, which is fine for this repo's Linux target but would break on BSD/macOS. More to the point, if that substitution ever produces empty output the arithmetic becomes a syntax error and the sweep exits non-zero having listed nothing useful, which is a poor failure mode for the one command whose job is finding leaked stacks. Latent rather than live: CloudFormation always returns a parseable ISO 8601 CreationTime, so there is no known input that triggers it today. Left unfixed as it is cosmetic against the reviewed change and the sweep's safety properties do not depend on the age column at all -- age is display-only and never feeds the teardown guard. Fix direction: compute the age in a guarded step and fall back to printing the raw timestamp when parsing fails.

findings.title: AppConfig.of applies base + derived defaults on the file path but not on the injected-context path, so the same app can see differently-shaped config
findings.detail: AppConfig.load (the file path) does deepMerge(getDefaultConfig(), file) then applyDerivedDefaults then validate. AppConfig.of on the injected-context path validates the raw context object with no base-defaults merge and no derived-defaults step. So an app run under the future 'cdk-cicd exec' (config arriving via cicd:config context) can see config lacking the removalPolicies RETAIN defaults and lacking CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT/_REGION derivation, while the same app under plain cdk deploy (config from file) sees them. This is only correct if the injecting wrapper pre-applies base+derived defaults before writing the context value, which is what accessor.ts's comment assumes. It is latent, not a present bug, because the injecting wrapper does not exist yet. Recorded so the M2 runtime-injection milestone (m2-register and friends) does not silently reintroduce the asymmetry: either the wrapper must resolve the full config (base + derived) before writing context, or AppConfig.of must run the same merge/derive pipeline on the context value that load runs on the file. Decide which at M2 and add a test that the two paths produce identical config for identical input.

findings.title: deepMerge assigns array-valued override keys by reference, so a later mutation of the parsed config would leak into an already-merged config
findings.detail: mergeRecords recurses into plain objects (which both clones and applies the UNSAFE_KEYS filter at depth) but assigns any non-plain-object value, including arrays, directly: result[key] = value. The deepMerge doc correctly says arrays replace rather than concatenate, and that is the intended semantics, but it does not clone them. The 'override object is not aliased into the result' test covers nested objects only, not arrays, so an array-valued key in the merged result is the same reference as in the caller's parsed object. Harmless today because the loader does not mutate the parsed config after merging and callers are not expected to either. It would become a real aliasing bug if any later code mutates a parsed config in place after AppConfig has returned. Fix direction if revisited: shallow-copy arrays on assignment (result[key] = value.slice() when Array.isArray(value)) and extend the aliasing test to an array-valued key.

findings.title: FieldKind.STRING_LIST validation checks only that the value is a non-empty array, not that its elements are strings
findings.detail: isMissing for STRING_LIST returns false as soon as the value is an array with length > 0, so a config value like [1, 2] or a mixed list satisfies a field declared STRING_LIST. This matches the enum member's documented semantics ('A non-empty array'), so it is very likely intentional rather than a defect, and tightening it would be a behaviour change that could reject configs that validate today. Recorded only so the choice stays conscious: if a later milestone relies on STRING_LIST fields actually being lists of strings (e.g. availabilityZones passed straight into a CDK construct that will throw on a non-string), either strengthen isMissing to check every element is a non-blank string or rename the kind to make the loose semantics explicit. No change now.

findings.title: The preload's construction-time config read sees a narrower context set than AppConfig.of, so a cicd:config in cdk.json drives the read side but not the injected tags/synthesizer
findings.detail: register.ts's readInjectedConfig runs before super(), when there is no App node, so it can only consult props.context and CDK_CONTEXT_JSON. The read side, AppConfig.of, reads the App's fully-merged context and its docstring notes cicd:config can also be hand-set in cdk.json's context field. So a cicd:config placed directly in cdk.json would be seen by AppConfig.of (used inside stacks) but would NOT drive the hook's tags/synthesizer, because the hook cannot read the cdk.json file pre-super without a node. This is fine for the supported path -- cdk-cicd exec (m2-exec) injects via CDK_CONTEXT_JSON, and command-line --context is merged into CDK_CONTEXT_JSON by the CDK CLI, so both are covered. It is an asymmetry to keep in mind when m2-exec is built and when documenting how config reaches the wrapper: the hook's inputs are CDK_CONTEXT_JSON + AppProps.context only. Fix direction if it ever bites: have exec normalise a cdk.json-level cicd:config into CDK_CONTEXT_JSON, or document that cdk.json-level cicd:config is read-only (consumed by AppConfig.of, not by injection).

findings.title: The multi-copy App patch does not check that the distinct aws-cdk-lib copies agree on version, so a dev/monorepo minor-version skew could silently misapply Aspects/tags
findings.detail: register.ts patches every distinct aws-cdk-lib copy reachable from the app entry / cwd / the hook, to survive workspaces that carry more than one copy. The cross-copy mechanism is sound for SAME-version copies: Aspects.of stores under Symbol.for('cdk-aspects') (a hardcoded global-registry key) and synthesis reads it back the same way, so the nested-copy applyWrapper and the root-copy synth share the same node metadata slot regardless of which copy's class created the App. All copies in this workspace are 2.195.0. The latent fragility: if two copies disagree on aws-cdk-lib minor version, data written by one copy's classes is read by another's synth logic, and interface drift (e.g. aspect-priority handling) could silently misbehave. Published installs are single-copy because aws-cdk-lib is a peerDependency, so this never affects users -- only dev/monorepo setups. Optional hardening: have distinctCdkCopies emit a warning (not throw) when the resolved copies' versions differ, so a skew is visible rather than silent. Not a correctness bug at the pinned version.

findings.title: CdkCicd.attach reuses markAppConstructed(), conflating an explicit attach with a wrapped-constructor App -- fine for today's diagnostic, revisit when m2-bundled-diagnostic is built
findings.detail: The construction counter (inject.ts markAppConstructed/appsConstructed) is named for Apps that pass through the wrapped constructor, but CdkCicd.attach also increments it so that an app which opts into attach counts as wrapped and the future bundled-app diagnostic stays silent. The counter's real semantic (appsConstructed = 'Apps the wrapper has wrapped') is satisfied and this is correct for the diagnostic's only current requirement (non-zero when the wrapper was applied). The coupling is baked in before m2-bundled-diagnostic exists: if that diagnostic later needs to distinguish an attach from constructor-wrapping (e.g. to warn that a non-bundled app called attach unnecessarily), this shared counter is too coarse and attach would need its own signal. Resolve when building m2-bundled-diagnostic: either keep the shared counter (if 'was the wrapper applied at all' stays the only question) or split into distinct construct-vs-attach counters. No change needed now.

findings.title: The CDK_CICD_EXEC arming flag is a cross-package contract exported only from an internal deep path, so m2-exec will likely duplicate the literal string
findings.detail: The bundled-app diagnostic arms only when process.env.CDK_CICD_EXEC === '1'. That flag is defined as EXEC_FLAG in the wrapper's internal src/v3/runtime/inject.ts, but its OTHER end -- the cdk-cicd exec launcher -- lives in the separate cdk-cicd-wrapper-cli package, which cannot import a non-exported deep runtime path (the jsii package's exports map does not publish it, and importing lib/v3/runtime/inject reaches past the public surface). So m2-exec will most likely hardcode the literal 'CDK_CICD_EXEC' a second time. Resolve when building m2-exec: either expose the flag name somewhere the CLI can import cleanly, or add a small test that asserts the two copies of the string agree, so a rename on one side cannot silently disarm the diagnostic on real runs.

findings.title: The bundled-diagnostic subprocess test depends on a compiled lib/ that the test task does not build, so it only passes after a separate compile step
findings.detail: bundled-diagnostic.test.ts runs the COMPILED preload (lib/v3/runtime/register.js) under node -r in a subprocess -- the only faithful way to exercise a process.on('exit') handler. But the projen 'test' task is jest + eslint with no compile step, and lib/ is gitignored, so a bare `npx jest` after a clean checkout would hit the test's beforeAll guard ('run npx projen compile first') and fail deterministically. It passes under the canonical `npm run build` (compile then test) and in this session because compile was run first. Not flaky, just order-dependent. Fix direction: have the wrapper's projen 'test' task spawn 'compile' first, or move the subprocess wiring test behind an integration-test task that depends on compile, so the standalone `npx jest` invocation is self-sufficient.

findings.title: The CLI's yargs usage breaks on yargs 18, which floated in on a projen regen and broke the entire CLI until yargs was pinned to ^17
findings.detail: src/index.ts does `import * as yargs from 'yargs'; const ya = yargs; ya.command(...)`. That namespace-as-instance pattern is a yargs v17 idiom; yargs 18 (released recently) changed its exports and `ya.command` is no longer a function, so `node lib/index.js` throws 'ya.command is not a function' and every CLI subcommand fails. This surfaced when enabling the wrapper dependency for m2-exec required a `npx projen` regen, which re-resolved the previously-unpinned `yargs` dep from 17.7.3 up to 18.0.0. Worked around by pinning `yargs@^17.7.3` + `@types/yargs@^17.0.33` in projenrc/CLIConfig.ts, which restores the working CLI and is the surgical fix. The real follow-up is to migrate the CLI's yargs bootstrap to the v18 API (call the factory / default import instead of the namespace) and then unpin, so the CLI can take yargs security updates. Out of scope for m2-exec, which only needed the CLI to run.

findings.title: level1-app/cicd.config.ts still carries a 'NOT ACTIVE YET -- defineCICD/Repository do not exist until wave 3' header, which is now false
findings.detail: As of m3-definecicd, defineCICD and Repository exist and the fixture's cicd.config.ts loads and normalizes via ts-node. Its header comment (lines ~4-8) still says the symbols do not exist until wave 3 and that the file is dormant, and the file is still listed in the fixture's tsconfig.json exclude. Left unchanged by the m3-definecicd unit on purpose (surgical scope): the file belongs to m3-config-discovery, which is the task that actually wires discovery/loading and should update the header (and decide whether to drop the tsconfig exclude) as part of activating it. Resolve when implementing m3-config-discovery: refresh the header to describe how the CLI discovers and loads the file, and remove the now-misleading 'not active' language.

findings.title: ts-node is required to load a .ts cicd.config (and by exec's -r ts-node/register) but is not a declared CLI dependency, so a global install can fail to resolve it
findings.detail: CicdConfig.load does an in-process require('ts-node/register') for a .ts config, and ExecCommand spawns node with -r ts-node/register for a .ts entry. ts-node resolves today only because it is hoisted into the workspace-root node_modules; it is NOT in the CLI package's dependencies. For a locally-installed CLI, in-process resolution walks up into the user's project and usually finds their ts-node; but a GLOBALLY-installed CLI (npm i -g) does not, so a user with a TypeScript cicd.config.ts (or a .ts app entry under exec) hits a module-resolution failure. Mitigated now: CicdConfig.load wraps the require in a clear, actionable error ('needs ts-node ... install it or compile to cicd.config.js') instead of a raw crash; the .ts path is unit-covered. The real fix is a distribution decision to make deliberately before external publish: declare ts-node as a CLI dependency in projenrc/CLIConfig.ts (pin the version to avoid a yargs-18-style float on regen), and apply the same clear-error treatment to the exec spawn path. Out of scope for m3-config-discovery's minimal change; track for the publish/harness-publish-loop work.
